articles.title: Arken Intermodal Terminal achieves near-doubled yard capacity
articles.summary: The Port of Gothenburg has significantly increased yard capacity at Arken Intermodal Terminal through a reconfiguration of the railway track layout, freeing up approximately 4,000 square metres of additional yard space for trailers and other units. articles.body: The Port of Gothenburg has significantly increased yard capacity at Arken Intermodal Terminal through a reconfiguration of the railway track layout, freeing up approximately 4,000 square metres of additional yard space for trailers and other units. The result is an increase of almost double the previous yard capacity from a five percent expansion in available space. Arken Intermodal Terminal is one of Sweden’s largest intermodal terminals and a key hub for transfers between rail, road and sea. Growing cargo volumes over time had pushed capacity in certain flows close to its limit, with yard space identified as the primary constraint. The capacity improvement was achieved by rebuilding one of the through tracks at the terminal to release the additional yard area, demonstrating that smarter use of existing infrastructure can deliver substantial gains without the need for large-scale construction. Carl Johan Andersson, Senior Logistics Developer at the Port of Gothenburg, described the result as an example of capacity development through intelligent use of existing land rather than simply building bigger, noting that a five percent increase in space has delivered close to a doubling of yard capacity. Emma Meltin, Bridge Manager Intermodal at Gothenburg RoRo Terminal, highlighted the operational benefits of greater yard flexibility, enabling better flow planning, more effective peak management and reduced unnecessary cargo movements, ultimately delivering more efficient and reliable service to customers.

articles.summary: By Heidi Taksdal Skjeseth and Alberto Nardelli Oct 19, 2026 (Bloomberg) –The European Union looks to be relaxing its opposition to oil and gas production in polar areas, while still calling...

(U.S. Navy Photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Alice Husted) By Heidi Taksdal Skjeseth and Alberto Nardelli Oct 19, 2026 (Bloomberg) –The European Union looks to be relaxing its opposition to oil and gas production in polar areas, while still calling for all fossil fuels to be kept in the ground in its forthcoming Arctic strategy. A draft of the strategy, seen by Bloomberg, contains no references to a moratorium on new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic, marking a shift in wording from the EU’s 2021 stance . The wording has been a topic of intense discussions between the trade bloc and Norway, which has lobbied hard for the EU to abandon its climate-based opposition to oil and gas exploration in the high north. The Nordic nation awarded five oil and gas exploration licenses in the Barents Sea , which is part of the Arctic, in last year’s licensing round and opened up 38 blocks in 2026 for applications. Norway supplied almost a third of EU’s gas imports last year, including a small part from those fields. The petroleum industry’s fear was that the EU would pledge not to buy oil and gas from Norway’s new Arctic fields. Instead, the draft says the union will “prioritize” renewable energy sources and hydrocarbons produced outside the Arctic. The European Commission also says it will work toward an international commitment to prevent further development of Arctic oil and gas resources, or purchases from them, when such activity “poses a threat to the Arctic ecosystem.” In 2021, the EU had said that “building on the partial moratoriums on hydrocarbons exploration in the Arctic” in parts of the US, Canada and Greenland, “the EU is committed to ensuring that oil, coal and gas stay in the ground, including in Arctic regions” and that it would work toward “a multilateral legal obligation not to allow any further hydrocarbon reserve development in the Arctic or contiguous regions, nor to purchase such hydrocarbons if they were to be produced.” The latest draft also reiterates the EU’s broader commitment to work toward keeping coal, oil and gas in the ground, including in the Arctic, in line with its climate targets. The bloc has set a legally binding goal of cutting net greenhouse gas emissions by 90% by 2040 from the 1990 level. Related Article; Shadow Fleet Traffic on Northern Sea Route Surges as Arctic Safety Concerns Grow A spokesperson for Equinor ASA, which already produces oil and gas and is exploring more fields in the Barents Sea — referred questions to the Energy Department, and a spokesperson for the ministry declined to comment ahead of the strategy’s release. Environmental groups said the changes don’t amount to a significant retreat by Brussels. Paal Frisvold, who heads the Alliance to Preserve the Moratorium on Oil Drilling in the Arctic, told Bloomberg that he believes that the omission of the word moratorium makes the key message on climate stronger, adding “EU is determined to keep fossil fuels in the ground.” The draft text also maintains the EU’s opposition to deep-sea mining until scientific knowledge gaps have been “satisfactorily filled.” Norway in 2024 approved seabed mining , although no such works have yet started. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: Cefetra has signed a ten-year agreement with Associated British Ports at the Port of Immingham, securing substantial storage space at the UK’s largest port by tonnage volume and reinforcing a partnership that spans nearly three decades. Cefetra is one of the UK and Ireland’s major traders of grains and animal feed raw materials, handling approximately five million tonnes of raw material annually with a turnover exceeding GBP 1 billion, supplying customers across the animal nutrition, food and drink industries including dairy, beef, poultry, pork and bakery sectors. The long-term contract provides Cefetra with a stable foundation for future planning and continued efficient movement of raw materials to the businesses that depend on them, while confirming Immingham’s strategic importance within the company’s UK supply network. Cefetra is part of Cefetra Group, which has more than 120 years of experience in agriculture and international trade. Paul Litten, Head of Commercial for ABP in the Humber, described the ten-year agreement as an important endorsement of the strategic role the Humber plays in UK supply chains, highlighting the combination of extensive storage capacity, efficient cargo handling and direct market access available at Immingham. James Neilson of Cefetra Ltd described the agreement as reflecting the company’s commitment to reliable customer service and expressed appreciation for the strong working relationship built with ABP and the Immingham team over the years. ABP’s four Humber ports of Immingham, Grimsby, Goole and Hull collectively form the UK’s leading trade gateway by volume, handling more than 50 million tonnes of cargo annually worth over GBP 60 billion.

articles.summary: Kongsberg Maritime reported a record order backlog of NOK 29.75 billion in the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong demand for newbuild vessels across several shipping segments. articles.body: Kongsberg Maritime reported a record order backlog of NOK 29.75 billion in the third quarter of 2026, supported by strong demand for newbuild vessels across several shipping segments. The Norwegian maritime technology company recorded order intake of NOK 8.32 billion during the quarter. This resulted in a book-to-bill ratio of 1.25, while its order backlog increased by NOK 1.35 billion compared with the previous quarter. Revenue reached NOK 6.64 billion, representing a 5% increase from the third quarter of 2025. Meanwhile, deliveries to newbuild vessels grew by 16%, although aftermarket revenue declined by 5%. Newbuild demand supports order growth Kongsberg Maritime reported EBITDA of NOK 1.04 billion, corresponding to a margin of 15.7%. The result included NOK 72 million in restructuring costs related to its ongoing competitiveness improvement programme. Lisa Edvardsen Haugan, President and CEO of Kongsberg Maritime, said strong contracting activity across several vessel segments had contributed to the company’s growing order backlog. “The third-quarter result demonstrate our continued ability to scale profitability on newbuild deliveries,” said Haugan. Newbuild orders remained strong during the quarter, with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.39. Offshore Energy, Naval & Government and Cargo represented the company’s largest vessel segments in terms of year-to-date order intake. According to Kongsberg Maritime, demand for integrated solutions continues to support its contracting activity. Shipowners are increasingly seeking technologies that improve vessel efficiency, reliability and operational performance. Following the end of the quarter, Kongsberg Maritime completed its acquisition of Swedish propulsion specialist Berg Propulsion AB on 1 October 2026. The acquisition expands the company’s propulsion and electrical systems portfolio. Berg Propulsion will become part of Kongsberg Maritime’s Propulsion & Handling division. Kongsberg Maritime expects its strong order backlog and continued demand for newbuild equipment to support future deliveries.

articles.title: Georgia Ports opens Gainesville inland port
articles.summary: Georgia Ports Authority has opened the Gainesville Inland Port in a grand opening ceremony attended by Governor Brian Kemp, Hall County dignitaries and Georgia Ports leadership. The US$ 134 million facility connects Northeast Georgia’s growing manufacturing and logistics corridor directly to the Port of Savannah via...
articles.body: Georgia Ports Authority has opened the Gainesville Inland Port in a grand opening ceremony attended by Governor Brian Kemp, Hall County dignitaries and Georgia Ports leadership. The US$ 134 million facility connects Northeast Georgia’s growing manufacturing and logistics corridor directly to the Port of Savannah via Norfolk Southern rail service, with an annual capacity of 200,000 containers and convenient truck access to interstates 85 and 985. Northeast Georgia represents a significant and expanding market, with a consumer base of 2 million, more than 300 manufacturers and 33% of the overall workforce concentrated in manufacturing, processing and logistics. Since 2020, 78 new and expanding firms have added more than 4,800 jobs and US$ 2 billion in capital investment to Gainesville-Hall County. The inland port is currently handling home and retail goods alongside manufacturing components for imports, with exports comprising farm and forest products and manufactured goods. Customers can choose between rail for greater affordability and heavier loads or truck-only service for faster transit. Georgia Ports Authority expects to shift 26,000 containers to rail in the terminal’s first year, reducing truck traffic on Atlanta and Georgia highways and improving emissions. The terminal links to the Port of Savannah’s 40 weekly vessel calls and will serve North Georgia and the Carolinas. As part of the development, Georgia Ports funded US$ 4.8 million in Hall County road projects, eliminating an at-grade rail crossing, rerouting White Sulphur Road to ensure unimpeded emergency vehicle access and resurfacing Cagle Road to provide an improved alternative route for local residents. Governor Kemp described the inland port as bringing the competitive advantage of Georgia’s port system directly to Northeast Georgia, easing highway congestion and connecting businesses to global markets. CEO Griff Lynch characterised Gainesville as a high-growth market where the inland port will improve supply chain performance and long-term customer competitiveness. The Gainesville facility is part of Georgia Ports’ US$ 5 billion ten-year infrastructure plan that also includes five additional container berths at Savannah, one RoRo berth at Brunswick and the US$ 2.3 billion Savannah Container Terminal scheduled to begin construction in 2028.

articles.title: Port of Antwerp-Bruges announces 2027 tariff adjustments
articles.summary: Port of Antwerp-Bruges has published its 2027 tariff adjustments covering both the Antwerp and Bruges-Zeebrugge port areas, with changes affecting vessel dues, environmental incentives, cruise ship charges, waste fees and concession tariffs. Towage tariffs in the Antwerp docks will increase by 3.57%, while Zeebrugge...
articles.body: Port of Antwerp-Bruges has published its 2027 tariff adjustments covering both the Antwerp and Bruges-Zeebrugge port areas, with changes affecting vessel dues, environmental incentives, cruise ship charges, waste fees and concession tariffs. Towage tariffs in the Antwerp docks will increase by 3.57%, while Zeebrugge platform towage dues are indexed in accordance with contractual agreements with Boluda at 2.65%. Across both port areas, the reduction on tonnage dues for double calls, covering consecutive calls at Antwerp and Zeebrugge, has been increased from 10 to 20%. The Environmental Ship Index discount mechanism has been reformed and standardised, abolishing the existing year-of-construction restriction in Antwerp and the minimum discount in Zeebrugge, with ESI scores from 45 to 70 attracting a 10% discount and scores above 70 up to 100 attracting a 15% discount. Harmonised reductions across both areas will apply to calls solely for bunkering for own use at 50 percent, bunker vessels at 75%, repairs or dry dock at 50%, empty-handed calls or degassing at 50%, crew changes at 50% and transit at EUR 0.4941 per GT. In the Antwerp port area, berthing dues for vehicles will be aligned with Zeebrugge tariffs from January 1, 2027 at EUR 0.1830 per tonne. In the Bruges-Zeebrugge port area, the permitted duration of stay is extended from 14 to 20 days in line with Antwerp, a fee of EUR 150 per hour is introduced for use of the RoRo bridge at quay 113, and drinking water fees are adjusted. Automotive tariffs continue phased GT adjustment with liner trade at EUR 0.1307 per GT and non-liner trade at EUR 0.2883 per GT from 2027. The maximum GT charged for containers increases from 175,000 to 200,000 GT. For cruise ships, new tariffs applicable from January 1, 2028 introduce a greening charge of EUR 4,000 per call, EUR 6,000 for first connection, a per-passenger greening charge of EUR 1.50, electricity consumption at EUR 0.31 per kWh and a EUR 1,000 discount per call when a vessel actually connects to shore power. Waste fees are adjusted at both locations from January 1, 2027. In Antwerp, the fixed fee will be EUR 400 per ship with a variable fee of EUR 0.027 per GT and a maximum of EUR 1,750. In Zeebrugge, the fixed fee will be EUR 150 per ship with a variable fee of EUR 0.011 per GT and a maximum of EUR 900. Concession tariffs will be indexed at 3.97 percent in line with the Consumer Price Index for August 2026. A new tariff of EUR 25.99 per square metre per year is introduced for battery energy storage system activities on concession land. From January 1, 2027, two additional fees will apply to reefer containers at the border inspection post on the left bank, covering use of the reefer monitoring system at EUR 9 per container per calendar day and out-of-hours repairs at EUR 1,000 per intervention for up to three hours.

U.S. Central Command/Handout via REUTERS By Gerry Doyle Oct 31, 2026 (Bloomberg) –As US President Donald Trump threatens renewed attacks against Iran, Tehran’s intermittent strikes on commercial vessels have left the two sides locked in a painful economic standoff. For Iran, the US blockade of its oil exports has snuffed out a key part of its military funding and severely hobbled the $300 billion economy, with only a tiny fraction of the prewar 2 million barrels per day are leaving the country via land routes. And for the US, the rising cost of shipping oil through the Strait of Hormuz — even though US Central Command says almost all Iranian attacks there fail or are intercepted — has kept fuel prices high, stirring a political backlash at home with the midterm elections fast approaching. Iran doesn’t even need a high tempo of attacks to keep oil prices elevated; although shipments through the strait are at about 80% of prewar levels, the associated risk has inflated insurance costs. It was more expensive in early October to hire a supertanker in some parts of the world than it was to send a rocket into space. But even significant economic pain isn’t likely to change Iran’s ability to keep up “ harassing fire ” in the strait, said Jim Lamson, a visiting research fellow in the Department of War Studies at King’s College London and former CIA analyst focused on Iran and the Middle East. A stockpile of missile components means Tehran can continue to assemble anti-ship weapons, even though US airstrikes have severely degraded its ability to manufacture them at scale, he said. “They have been planning for a long-term asymmetric conflict with the US for decades,” Lamson said. “Things like building in resilience, building in redundancy, building in stockpiling — these have been part of their military culture.” Although there have been a record of at least 28 open-source reports of damage to shipping in the strait in October, Iran has not increased its volume of attacks, according to a US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Instead, more serious damage has led to more incidents being flagged, with a quarter of the reports in the first two weeks of October involving strikes on ships’ engine rooms, which can take vessels out of service. The continued attacks by Iran leave a few options — none of them with a guaranteed favorable outcome. Trump may order the resumption of airstrikes after the election, even though these only go so far to completely shut down Iran’s ability to lob missiles into the strait — typically unsophisticated weapons that attack any ship in a target area. That leaves making the economic cost of Iranian ship attacks impossible to bear, said John Miller, a retired US Navy vice admiral and former head of CENTCOM. “As long as they want to have a blockade in place, they can continue to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz,” Miller said of Iran. “This has always been the case: You can either make them unwilling or unable.” The tanker industry is continuing to send oil out of the Middle East for now at near prewar levels, and it’s not clear what sort of escalation it would take to halt that. Transits through the waterway are earning owners of supertankers tens of millions of dollars, and the vessels’ crews several months’ pay for a few days of dangerous navigation. For now that’s proving sufficient to keep trade running. The International Maritime Organization estimates that there have been 121 incidents in Hormuz and the wider region since the war began, including 24 confirmed seafarer fatalities. Read Also: Containership Sinks as Hormuz Attacks Spiral Out of Control No ship has struck a floating min e while transiting the strait, the US official said, although Iran said as recently as late October that a mine damaged a tanker, and on Friday the UKMTO, which monitors shipping security, reported a tanker was damaged by explosives placed on its hull. Iran is using both traditional cruise missiles and drones to attack shipping, the official said, and US forces are both organizing ship transits and protecting them, largely with aircraft overhead. CENTCOM has said about 95% of ships transit the strait without incident. The US works directly with the shipping industry, sharing information and discussing timing, routes and numbers for vessels that want to pass through the strait in either direction, the US official said. US forces then formulate a plan for doing so safely, including what assets will be used to keep tabs on the journey and shoot down threats if necessary. Miller said much of Iran’s ability to track anything beyond visual range of its shores had been all but destroyed over the last eight months. As a result, the weapons it uses are often fired blind, or at the general area where Iranian strike planners think ships might be. Once the missiles arrive, radar or infrared seekers guide them to whatever is nearby. Aircraft armed with cheap munitions such as the APKWS missile, which costs about $20,000 for a BAE Systems Plc guidance kit, handle those sorts of attacks. The expensive and advanced air-defense interceptors on US Navy ships, such as the Raytheon SM-6 and SM-3 Block IIA, are then reserved for ballistic missile threats. Trump has previewed in recent days plans for renewed attacks on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. But it’s not clear that airstrikes — especially against an adversary that has planned for decades to keep key capabilities safe against such attacks — will change the situation in the strait, said Emma Salisbury, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and an associate fellow at the Royal Navy Strategic Studies Centre. A surge in fighting could push oil prices into the $120-$130 range, according to analysis by Bloomberg Economics chief emerging markets economist Ziad Daoud. Both sides “may prefer a brief conflict to improve their negotiating power,” he wrote. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Ann Wang TAIPEI, Nov 1 (Reuters) – China’s Coast Guard is harassing shipping with its latest patrol off Taiwan’s east coast and trying to exert a fictional jurisdiction, the Taiwanese Coast Guard said, adding it had sent its own ships to keep watch. China, which views Taiwan as its own territory, has stepped up activity off the island’s east coast since June with regular coast guard patrols. Officials in Taiwan, which rejects Beijing’s sovereignty ?claims, say they believe China is practicing for a potential maritime blockade using overlapping military, paramilitary and civilian assets. Taipei regards the area off its east ?coast as critical to wartime supply routes from allies in the event of a blockade or conflict. China recognizes no claims of sovereignty by Taiwan. Responding late Saturday to China’s announcement of its latest east coast patrol, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said two Chinese ships were involved and it had sent its own forces to monitor. Chinese state media showed video of one of its ships broadcasting a radio message that it was carrying out law enforcement and offering help should any be needed. It did not say who the message was broadcast at, but showed footage of an unidentified fishing trawler. Taiwan’s Coast Guard said China’s “attempts to harass ships at sea through radio communications are a clear expansion of power that violate international law, undermine regional peace and stability, and deviate from reality.” “Our country holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the exclusive economic zone east of Taiwan, and China has absolutely no jurisdiction over any of Taiwan’s waters,” it added. China on Saturday also sent another Coast Guard ship close to the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands, which are strategically located at the top of the South China Sea, Taiwan’s Coast Guard said separately. Taiwan has so far this year “expelled” Chinese Coast Guard vessels from Pratas waters 13 times, it added. The Pratas have no permanent civilian population and lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong. Security experts see them as vulnerable to Chinese attack due to their ?distance — more than 400 km (250 ?miles) — from Taiwan. (Reporting by Ben Blanchard; editing by Lincoln Feast.) In its latest statement, the IRGC Navy said a fourth vessel, a tanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude oil, had hit a mine, suffered a powerful explosion and was burning. articles.title: Ramble On: Who Pays the Freight?
articles.summary: In September we borrowed a Led Zeppelin title to describe China’s crude stockpile, a levee holding backthe import shortfall created by the closure of Hormuz. One month on, the wateris still falling, Gulf crude has rambled on around the Strait, and the questionis what it will cost to rebuild. China’s customs...
articles.body: Ramble On: Who Pays the Freight? in International Shipping News 31/10/2026 In September we borrowed a Led Zeppelin title to describe China’s crude stockpile, a levee holding backthe import shortfall created by the closure of Hormuz. One month on, the wateris still falling, Gulf crude has rambled on around the Strait, and the questionis what it will cost to rebuild. China’s customs crudeimports were 9.03 mbpd in September, broadly flat on August, while refineryruns climbed to 13.99 mbpd, the highest since March. Hence China drew on itsstocks for the fourth time in five months, a net 0.60 mbpd after crude exports (Figure1). Of the 121.5 million barrels built by April, only 31 million remain. At theMay to September pace of 0.59 mbpd, that would be gone by late November.Arrivals picked up in October, but those cargoes were bought in the summer, andwith Brent around US$ 100 since early September, the refill is likely to slow. From the Red Sea to the relay: two bypasses in six months The levee was needed because the Gulf’s main exit closed. Our data shows that crude loaded directly inside the Strait of Hormuz fell from about 14 mbpd in January and February to under 1 mbpd in September. China felt it first, with customs imports dropping from 12.0 mbpd in January and February to 7.1 mbpd in June, and the gap was met from tanks. However, Gulf crude kept moving, and it changed route twice. Between March and July the Red Sea carried the load, with Saudi crude piped across the Peninsula and loaded at Yanbu and Rabigh, a route that peaked at about 4.3 mbpd in June, against about 0.8 mbpd before the war. The attack on the East-West pipeline in August threw a spanner in the works. The weight shifted back east, and crude now crosses the Strait on tankers, some of them on dark transits, before being transferred ship to ship onto VLCCs off Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and Sohar. This relay grew from almost nothing in February to about 5 mbpd in September, while loadings at Fujairah’s berths and Oman’s own ports carried a further 3.9 mbpd. By September, loadings at the hub ports had risen to about 8.5 mbpd, five times their 2025 level, and briefly ran close to 12 mbpd in the last week of the month. Where the barrels went Meanwhile, the cheapest barrels have gone. After the US blockade in April, Iranian crude largely stopped leaving the Gulf, and the Iranian barrels floating off Malaysia and Singapore are close to exhausted by our count (Figure 2). China’s choice narrows to its stockpile or Gulf crude. Why has freight not decided where Asia buys? VLCC earnings on the MEG/China route (TD3C) moved from parity with West Africa/China (TD15) in January and February to 4.2 times TD15 in May, and averaged US$ 1.02 million/day TCE in September, 17.5 times their 2025 average (Figure 3). On earnings alone, the Atlantic looked the obvious alternative, unless the crude could be loaded outside the Strait, on the Gulf of Oman route (TD34). However, earnings overstate what the buyer pays. At the Baltic’s standard speeds of 13 knots laden and 12 knots in ballast, a VLCC needs about 46 days for the round voyage from Ras Tanura to Ningbo, against about 76 days from West Africa, so the lower daily rate on TD15 is billed for longer. Take a VLCC carrying about 2 million barrels to Ningbo in September. Loaded at Ras Tanura, inside the Strait, the cargo paid about US$ 52 million in freight, or US$ 26/bbl. Loaded in West Africa it paid about US$ 35 million, or US$ 17.5/bbl, even though TD3C earned 2.5 times as much per day as TD15. Loaded at Mina al Fahal in Oman, outside the Strait, it paid about US$ 30 million, or US$ 15/bbl, the cheapest of the three. By October the order was the same and the gaps wider: about US$ 34/bbl from Ras Tanura, US$ 28 from West Africa and US$ 19 from Mina al Fahal. Furthermore, as the relay off Fujairah, priced on TD34, took over after the pipeline attack, China’s imports recovered with it. The TD3C premium, in turn, priced the difficulty of leaving the Gulf. Whenever a route out of the Gulf opened, Asia bought. Our numbers show who paid that premium: cargoes loaded inside the Strait, on TD3C, and buyers avoided those wherever they could. A VLCC loading in the Gulf of Oman, meanwhile, cost less to send to China than one loading in West Africa. Crude prices set how much it bought: Brent rose from US$ 72.48 before the war to an intraday high of about US$ 126 on 30 April, and Chinese buying only recovered once it fell below US$ 80 in the summer. Gulf producers’ discounts, and the fit of Gulf medium sour grades with Asia’s complex refineries, explain why buyers returned so quickly. What it means for tonnage Every cargo that crosses the Strait on one tanker and is reloaded onto another off Oman ties up two vessels and adds waiting time at the transfer point. September showed the first sustained sign of demand pulling on that system, as freight for VLCCs loading in the Gulf of Oman (TD34) tripled m-o-m, faster than TD3C inside the Strait. Attacks on tankers crossing the Strait at the end of September did not stop the trade. In October the shortage reached the Atlantic. The number of VLCCs ballasting towards West Africa, Brazil and the US Gulf fell from about 85 a week in early September to 50 to 54 since mid-October, while transfers off Oman ran at their limits. TD15 rose 60% m-o-m in Worldscale, against 26% for TD34, taking West African earnings to US$ 667,000/day. The bill comes due The September loadings now on the water will reach China in October and November, just as the stock build runs out. China is still buying from the Atlantic, with 19 VLCCs fixed from Brazil and West Africa to China in the last ten days of October, most of them loading in November. Should the transfer network off Oman keep pace, Gulf crude will carry the refill and keep drawing tonnage east, supporting earnings on both routes. Should it falter, China will have to choose between drawing deeper into a stockpile estimated at more than a billion barrels and buying from further away, at a higher freight cost per barrel. Either way, the cost of moving a barrel to Asia has become part of the price of the barrel itself. More specifically, the shipbroker noted that “the shipbuilding market has moved from an ordering boom into a delivery wave. The total orderbook for...
articles.body: Tanker Orders Leading Newbuilding Activity With Prices Expected to Remain High Throughout 2027 in Hellenic Shipping News 31/10/2026 T anker ordering activity has been leading the latest surge of contracting, despite high prices, Banchero Costa said in a new research report focused on newbuilding. More specifically, the shipbroker noted that “the shipbuilding market has moved from an ordering boom into a delivery wave. The total orderbook for bulkcarriers, tankers, LNG and LPG carriers and containerships stands at 179.1 mln CGT, 25.0% more than a year earlier (143.3 mln CGT) and the largest in the last 20 years. Containerships account for 38% of it, ahead of bulkcarriers (18%) and LNG carriers (16%). Relative to the fleet it is largest for containerships (43.5%), LNG carriers (40.9%), LPG carriers (38.5%) and crude tankers (29.3%), against 14.2% for bulkcarriers. The orderbook for bulkcarriers and crude and product tankers stands at 2,700 ships and 326.5 mln DWT, or 19.1% of the fleet, 41% more than a year ago and 2.7 times its 2021 level. Yard capacity is the main constraint. Chinese yards hold 75% of the bulkcarrier and tanker orderbook and are scheduled to deliver 89.1 mln DWT of these ships in 2028, against their record of 62.6 mln DWT in 2011”. According to Banchero Costa, “contracting has been driven by tankers. In Jan-Sep 2026, 267 crude tankers of 67.0 mln DWT were ordered (+267.7% y-o-y), including 172 VLCCs, while bulkcarrier ordering held steady (+4.7% in DWT terms). 83 LNG carriers of 13.12 mln CBM were ordered, against 35 of 2.94 mln CBM a year earlier, and 519 containerships of 4.05 mln TEU (+11.7%), 89% of them at Chinese yards”. Additionally, “newbuilding prices are firm for tankers and bulkcarriers but softer for large containerships and LNG carriers. In Sep 2026 a VLCC was assessed at USD 131.0 mln (+7.4% y-o-y) and a Capesize at USD 79.0 mln (+3.9%), while a 20,000 TEU containership eased to USD 210.4 mln (-4.8%) and a 180,000 CBM LNG carrier to USD 242.0 mln (-3.3%). We expect tanker newbuilding prices to stay firm into 2027, with the main yards full until 2029, but see limited room for further gains as new Chinese capacity comes on stream. With 33% of this year’s contracting (in CGT) at new or revived yards, the main risks are delays and the 2028 delivery peak”, the shipbroker said. THE ORDERBOOK: LARGEST FOR CONTAINERSHIPS, GAS CARRIERS AND TANKERS Banchero Costa added that “the orderbook is large in every cargo sector, but its size relative to the fleet differs widely. Bulkcarriers of 20,000 DWT and over have 1,449 ships and 145.3 mln DWT on order (14.2% of the trading fleet), crude tankers of 60,000 DWT and over 574 ships and 135.4 mln DWT (29.3%), coated product tankers of 30,000-119,999 DWT 677 ships and 45.9 mln DWT (20.7%), and IMO I/II chemical tankers of 1,000-41,999 DWT 540 ships (20.2%). Containerships and gas carriers have the largest orderbooks relative to their fleets. 1,641 fully cellular containerships of 14.6 mln TEU are on order, equal to 43.5% of the fleet, and the ULCS orderbook equals 87% of the ULCS fleet. For LNG carriers the ratio is 40.9% (350 ships of 54.9 mln CBM) and for LPG carriers 38.5% (320 ships of 21.4 mln CBM), with the VLGC orderbook at 44.6% of the VLGC fleet”. Meanwhile, during the past week, Banchero Costa noted that “newbuilding activity this week was broad-based, with significant contracting across the bulk carrier, container, tanker, gas carrier and offshore sectors. articles.body: Suezmax Tanker sales surge 35% amid high VLCC demand in International Shipping News 31/10/2026 A strong VLCC market this year is boosting Suezmax Tanker demand. Suezmax sales activity has picked up considerably in recent months, with sales so far this year up 35%, reaching 124 sales compared to 92 sales over the same period last year. Buyers have continued to transact even as values have climbed, pointing to strong sector demand. Both values and timecharter rates are now at an all-time high, with one year timecharter rates four times higher than this time last year, adding to the momentum behind sales and keeping buyer and seller interest firmly focused on the sector. The average age of vessels sold is 15 years. On the buying side, Greece has been the biggest buyer with 21% of purchases, followed by the UAE with 15% and China in third place with 8%. Greece has also been active on the selling side, accounting for 33% of sales, including nine Suezmax vessels sold by Dynacom this year. China is in second place with 9% of sales and Belgium in third with 6%, as CMB.Tech and Exmar offloaded eight vessels combined. Notable recent sales include the Suezmax Achilleas (158,400 DWT, Jun 2010, Hyundai Heavy Industries Ulsan) sold by Sun Enterprises for USD 98.0 mil, VV Value USD 100.47 mil. Also the Suezmax Maran Poseidon (158,300 DWT, Jan 2010, Hyundai Heavy Industries Ulsan) sold by Maran Tankers for USD 98.5 mil, VV Value USD 101.88 mil. What’s Driving the Demand? As VLCC values have risen this year, it has inadvertently pushed up demand for the considerably cheaper Suezmax Tanker segment. As attention has transferred from VLCCs to Suezmax Tankers, strong buying and higher earnings have pushed values up significantly across all size ranges, narrowing the price gap between the two, though not as sharply as VLCC values have risen. Older Suezmax vessels have seen the biggest gains, with a 15YO 160,000 DWT Suezmax up c.134.58% since the start of the year, from USD 45.6 mil to USD 106.97 mil. The scale of the move for older tonnage shows how quickly pricing across the age spectrum has reset in a matter of months. Earnings have moved in the same direction. One-year timecharter rates are up by 301% year on year, from 40,151 USD/day to 161,054 USD/day. Disruptions to normal trading patterns have made reliable tonnage harder to find, and with demand for Suezmax Tankers rising at the same time, owners have been able to command significantly higher rates for longer commitments. A one-year timecharter now locks in earnings at a level that would have been hard to imagine twelve months ago, which helps explain why values have followed rates higher. Sellers are also looking to capitalise on these gains, with the combination of firm earnings and rising asset values shaping activity in the sector. Part of the appeal of Suezmax Tankers is their versatility. Unlike VLCCs, they can transit the Suez Canal fully laden, which opens up a direct route between the Middle East, the Mediterranean and Europe and avoids the longer passage around the Cape of Good Hope. The Tankers’ size also gives them access to a wider range of ports and terminals than VLCCs, giving charterers more flexibility in the trades they can serve. With VLCC values and earnings already elevated and vessels in short supply due to strong demand, Suezmaxes offer a more flexible and cheaper alternative within the Tanker market. Activity in the sector will be one to watch in the coming weeks. Source: Veson Nautical Tops 2026-10-31 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: China charts course for green corridors
articles.summary: China is emerging as an influential player in the global green shipping corridor movement, leveraging its dominance in green fuel production, battery technology and maritime infrastructure to take a leading role in efforts to decarbonise international shipping. Yet despite holding advantages across much of the value...
articles.body: China charts course for green corridors in International Shipping News , Shipping: Emission Possible 31/10/2026 C hina is emerging as an influential player in the global green shipping corridor movement, leveraging its dominance in green fuel production, battery technology and maritime infrastructure to take a leading role in efforts to decarbonise international shipping. Yet despite holding advantages across much of the value chain, the country still faces significant challenges if it is to convert ambition into commercially viable zero-emission trade routes. A report from the Global Maritime Forum on China’s progress with green shipping corridors noted that China was involved in at least 21 green corridor initiatives as of June 2026, representing “nearly a fifth of the global green corridor portfolio”. According to the report, China possesses strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks needed to successfully develop green shipping corridors: viable zero-emission fuel pathways, cross-value-chain collaboration and an enabling policy environment. Customer demand remains the weakest link. “China holds strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks necessary to successfully realise green corridors,” the report said. It adds that the country is positioning itself “as a leading supplier of three zero-emission fuels and technologies central to the advancement of green corridors: methanol, ammonia, and electric batteries”. That strength is built on China’s rapid expansion in green methanol and ammonia production, coupled with its emergence as a global leader in marine battery technology. The report highlights the country’s “low cost and early availability of green methanol and ammonia” and its position “at the forefront of marine battery development” as key competitive advantages. At the same time, China benefits from “innovative commercial partnerships and knowledge-sharing platforms across the value chain” and “rapidly strengthening policies related to green hydrogen”. Green avenues The report says that successfully developing green corridors could help China scale strategic hydrogen and battery industries, gain market share in a global bunker market worth approximately $100bn and participate in a wider maritime decarbonisation investment pipeline valued at between $1tn and $2tn. It could also support as many as four million green jobs while helping future-proof Chinese shipyards and maritime labour against the energy transition. However, the report stresses that major barriers remain. For example, there are gaps in both “soft” and “hard” infrastructure, including fuel certification systems, bunkering networks and charging infrastructure. It also points to the risk of competition for green ammonia from domestic industries, difficulties maintaining alignment across corridor partnerships, high costs associated with alternative fuels and battery-electric vessels, and what it describes as “fragmented global demand for zero-emission shipping services”. But the overarching challenge is economic. While China may currently offer some of the lowest-cost green methanol and ammonia globally, those fuels remain significantly more expensive than conventional marine fuels. Likewise, battery-powered vessels still carry substantial capital cost premiums. The report warns that customer demand has not developed at the same pace as supply-side initiatives. While some cargo owners are willing to pay higher freight rates for lower-carbon transport, willingness to absorb green fuel premiums remains inconsistent across markets. This creates uncertainty for project developers, shipowners and fuel producers attempting to make large-scale investments. Against this backdrop, the report’s recommendations section focuses on a set of practical measures that could help move Chinese corridors from planning into operation. Points for success The first recommendation calls for accelerated development of infrastructure supporting methanol, ammonia and battery-electric shipping. The report argues that progress is needed in both certification frameworks and physical logistics networks. “This can be split into two focal points: soft infrastructure, aligning fuel projects with global certification standards, and hard infrastructure, the rollout of physical fuel transportation and bunkering networks,” the report noted. “Both are necessary to connect China’s green fuel production with the global shipping sector.” Alignment with international standards is viewed as particularly important for routes linking China and Europe. The report notes that compatibility with the EU’s Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin framework will be essential if shipping companies are to maximise regulatory compliance benefits under European legislation. The second recommendation focuses on governance and collaboration. Drawing on lessons from green corridor projects around the world, the report says successful initiatives tend to share several traits, including clear governance structures, technology-focused targets, detailed feasibility studies and comprehensive implementation roadmaps. The report also suggests that China can shorten development timelines by building on partnerships that already exist around fuel production, bunkering and offtake agreements. Rather than creating entirely new structures, corridor developers may be able to use existing commercial relationships as the foundation for broader decarbonisation projects. A third recommendation centres on policy intervention to close the cost gap between conventional and zero-emission fuels. “Both national and international policy action will be needed to support the success of green corridors,” the report says. The authors argue that corridors connected to Europe already benefit from demand signals created by the EU Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime regulations. They also point to growing domestic support mechanisms in China, including green fuel incentives and hydrogen pilot programmes that could lower fuel costs and encourage early deployment. Creating partnerships Looking ahead, the report suggests there is scope for bilateral and plurilateral cooperation with major trading partners including the EU, Singapore, Australia and the United States. Mechanisms such as H2Global are highlighted as potential models for supporting green fuel deployment across international trade routes. The final recommendation addresses what may prove the most difficult challenge: creating customer demand. “Customer demand can be leveraged by targeting the shipping sectors that have demonstrated a higher willingness to pay and/or aggregating mechanisms,” the report argues. The authors recommend focusing on first-mover industries with established climate commitments, particularly participants in the iron ore, vehicle and container sectors. Engaging cargo-owner alliances such as the Zero-Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance could also help consolidate demand and improve willingness to pay for green shipping services. Meanwhile, domestic policy measures aimed at reducing shipping carbon intensity among China’s state-owned enterprises may provide an additional source of early demand. In its conclusion, the report presents a clear assessment of China’s position within the global maritime energy transition. “With a portfolio that represents nearly one-fifth of global initiatives and international collaboration as a national priority, China is well-positioned to lead the development of green shipping corridors,” the report concludes. It adds that China has “clear strengths across three of the four key building blocks required to make green corridors a success”, citing fuel availability, policy support and supply-chain collaboration. Source: Baltic Exchange Tops 2026-10-31 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Yet despite holding advantages across much of the value chain, the country still faces significant challenges if it is to convert ambition into commercially viable zero-emission trade routes.
Customer demand remains the weakest link.
“China holds strategic advantages in three of the four building blocks necessary to successfully realise green corridors,” the report said.

articles.body: Sanctioned Iran-Linked Tankers Went Dark Over Gulf of Oman Cables as the IRGC Threatened Them in International Shipping News 31/10/2026 Seven Cable Systems Run Through the Corridor The waters off Oman’s Batinah coast carry one of the densest concentrations of undersea cables in the region. Seven systems pass through the corridors where the three tankers operated, namely 2Africa, Bay of Bengal Gateway (BBG), Asia Africa Europe-1 (AAE-1), the Oman Australia Cable (OAC), Europe India Gateway (EIG), Transworld (TW1), and SeaMeWe-4. Between them, these cables connect Oman, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain, Iraq, Pakistan, India, Sri Lanka, Egypt, and Europe, with OAC running onward to Australia. Their owners include Meta, Vodafone, Orange, AT&T, Verizon, BT, China Mobile, China Telecom, Reliance Jio, Omantel, e&, and many of the region’s major telecom operators. Damage here would ripple well beyond the Gulf. Loops, U-Turns, and Days in the Dark A Loop and an 86-Hour Blackout Off Sohar On October 14 and 15, CELESTIAL SEA (IMO 9397030), a U.S.-sanctioned, Iran-flagged products tanker, drifted in a loop for 4.3 hours at 0 to 1.4 knots, 0.65 nautical miles from the 2Africa corridor. On October 15, it went dark inside the 2Africa and BBG corridors off Sohar. It stayed dark for 86 hours and came back transmitting only about 9 nautical miles from where it went dark. When it reappeared on October 19, it made a U-turn above BBG and then anchored off Shinas. The tanker was in ballast throughout, according to Vortexa data. A Laden Gas Carrier Turns Away From Malaysia A U.S.-sanctioned very large gas carrier (VLGC) was anchored next to CELESTIAL SEA. On October 23, the VLGC left Shinas for Pasir Gudang in Malaysia, laden with about 494,500 barrels of LPG, according to Vortexa data. Ten hours later, it slowed below 3 knots for 42 minutes inside the 2Africa corridor, with OAC and BBG 2.5 to 4 nautical miles away. It then turned 180 degrees back toward Oman, away from its destination, and went dark about 2 nautical miles from AAE-1. As of October 28, it had been dark for five days. Ten Days Loitering Between Jask and Chabahar The third tanker, an Iran-flagged very large crude carrier (VLCC) in ballast according to Vortexa data, loitered at under 1 knot for about 10 days in Iran’s EEZ between Jask and Chabahar, 0.4 to 3 nautical miles from the EIG, TW1, BBG, and SeaMeWe-4 routes. It went dark repeatedly, including for 33 hours from October 17. On October 18, it met an Iran-flagged vessel with no IMO number. It has been dark since October 26. Three Tankers With Direct Ties to Iran’s State and Military All three tankers are part of Iran’s sanctioned oil trade. CELESTIAL SEA was sanctioned by OFAC in April 2025, under its former name HARMONY, as part of the fleet of a UAE-based operator whose vessels moved oil for the National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) and, in 2023, for the Iranian military, according to the U.S. Treasury. The operator also worked with associates of a Houthi financial official. The tanker has used an Iranian call sign and an Iranian MMSI, and it swapped identities with another tanker in August 2025. In May, U.S. Marines boarded it in the Gulf of Oman on suspicion of trying to break the U.S. blockade. The VLCC flies Iran’s flag and is operated by the National Iranian Tanker Company (NITC), the state tanker company. Treasury sanctioned NITC in 2020, together with the Petroleum Ministry and NIOC, for funding the IRGC Quds Force. The VLCC’s registered owner is also listed by the UK and EU. The tanker has broadcast two other names and has met the same Iran-flagged vessel about nine times since August. The VLGC was sanctioned in April 2026, together with its Panama-based owner, for carrying about two million barrels of Iranian LPG since early 2025, according to Treasury. It changed its MMSI and call sign in May and June, took on a Vietnamese operator, and was dark for 877 hours in August and September. At the Shinas anchorage, both the VLGC and CELESTIAL SEA met other vessels. A Fishing-Support Vessel Worked the Same Cables The pattern is not confined to the sanctioned tanker fleet. A 34-meter Iran-flagged general cargo vessel that Windward tags as part of a fishing support fleet resumed transmitting on October 5 in the offshore Gulf of Oman southeast of Jask, in an area it had never entered in its AIS record since November 2024. After a stop about one kilometer off the Iranian Makran coast on October 8, it went dark for almost twelve days in the same area. From October 21 to 24, it loitered at 0.1 to 0.5 knots along the EIG and TW1 routes, moving back up-current at about 3 knots and drifting again, passing over EIG on October 22 and holding 0.4 to 1.7 nautical miles from TW1 for roughly 30 hours on October 23 and 24. On October 25, it crossed FALCON and the UAE-Iran cable off Jask, then sailed north into Iranian waters. It has been dark since October 26. Its ownership is opaque. The owner and manager operate only this vessel, and its beneficial owner has been unknown since August 2025. Windward assesses its IUU fishing risk as High. Nothing public ties the company to the Iranian state. Two things are worth noting alongside that. Fishing in Iranian waters requires a licence from the state fisheries company Shilat, per FAO and UNEP. And the IRGC Navy has organized fishermen and their boats into a naval Basij that its commander described as a shadow navy, in which people enter the battle with their own vessels. Iran has used civilian and commercial hulls for intelligence collection before. The IRISL-owned SAVIZ and BEHSHAD, both registered as cargo ships, served as IRGC intelligence platforms passing targeting data to the Houthis. On October 6, U.S. forces destroyed an Iranian-linked dhow in the Gulf of Oman that CENTCOM said was conducting surveillance on U.S. Navy ships, and the IRGC has turned to unarmed spotters on small boats to identify targets. The area is a busy fishing ground. What does not fit that explanation is a small vessel with a concealed beneficial owner working slowly along two cable routes in waters it had never visited, during the weeks the IRGC was threatening those cables. Iran Threatened the Cables in the Same Weeks The three tankers worked the cable corridors in the same weeks Iran threatened the cables. On October 12, two days before CELESTIAL SEA’s loop, Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that cables and data centers across the region could be attacked if the war resumes. On October 19, IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi said seven major internet cables run under Hormuz and that this time Iran’s response would be much harsher. On October 21, Yadollah Javani, political deputy to the IRGC chief commander, warned that attacks on Iranian infrastructure could bring retaliation against the Hormuz cables, according to Tasnim. On October 23, the day the VLGC slowed and turned back on 2Africa, two senior Iranian security officials noted that Tehran has detailed plans to target the Gulf’s undersea cables if the U.S. and Israel attack Iran again, and would try to prevent repairs to prolong the outage. Iran already uses merchant vessels for intelligence and military operations. The IRGC used two cargo ships belonging to the state-owned Islamic Republic of Iran Shipping Lines (IRISL) off Yemen to support the Houthis, including passing them targeting data and vessel tracks. Earlier this month, two other sanctioned Iran-linked tankers drifted for days over the same corridors. Iran-affiliated channels have also circulated an AI-generated video threatening to cut the Gulf’s cables, pushed by accounts assessed as troll operations. The provenance is unestablished, but the amplification places the threat in the information space alongside the official statements. Why Cargo Logistics Don’t Explain the Moves Vessels waiting off Shinas sit near the cables anyway, but cargo logistics don’t explain these moves. The VLCC and CELESTIAL SEA were empty, so their days of loitering were not floating storage. The VLGC was laden with a cargo already ordered to Malaysia, and it turned back off Muscat, far from the U.S. blockade line, right after slowing on the 2Africa corridor. CELESTIAL SEA went dark over two corridors and came back transmitting 86 hours later only 9 nautical miles away, rather than waiting at the anchorage. The fishing-support vessel carried no cargo rationale at all. It drifted at under half a knot along two cable routes in an area outside its two-year operating history, then left. For vessels from networks that already work for Iran’s state and military, that fits the profile of mapping the cable routes, or of placing charges or mines on them while dark, ahead of the attacks Tehran says it has planned. What to Watch Three of four tankers remain dark, and where and when they reappear will show whether the cable corridors were the destination or a stop along the way. Further loitering by sanctioned Iran-linked tankers over the Batinah corridors, especially alongside new IRGC statements on the cables, would confirm a pattern rather than a coincidence. Source: Windward 2026-10-31 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: GMS Week 44 – Buyers Raise The Stakes in Weekly Demolition Reports 31/10/2026 Last week’s recovery in dry freight offered recycling buyers little encouragement. This week, however, sentiment has improved across the sub-continent, with recyclers showing greater willingness to compete for available tonnage. Bangladesh continues to lead the market, while Pakistan and India are also displaying renewed confidence. Despite improving buying interest, the shortage of suitable recycling candidates persists as owners continue to benefit from attractive trading alternatives. The Strait of Hormuz supplied another reminder of the fragile security environment surrounding Gulf shipping. A tanker was attacked near Khasab, Oman, on October 29, reportedly sustaining an engine-room fire before resuming its voyage. The incident renewed concerns over passage security and insurance costs. For ageing tanker owners, disrupted trading patterns and restricted effective vessel availability continue to support employment opportunities rather than encourage recycling decisions. Oil markets responded to the renewed uncertainty. Brent advanced above USD 117 per barrel on Friday, while WTI approached USD 104 as concerns over Middle Eastern supplies persisted. Elevated energy costs continue to pressure recycling operations and steel production, particularly across the sub-continent. Yet the same uncertainty can support tanker earnings, keeping older vessels commercially attractive for longer than recyclers would prefer. Dry freight offered mixed signals. The Baltic Dry Index edged higher from 2,693 last Thursday to 2,712 on October 29, supported by Capesizes strengthening to 4,090. Panamaxes, however, weakened to 1,921, while Supramaxes eased to 1,870. The divergence suggests that pressure is emerging in selected vessel segments without producing a broader deterioration in earnings. For recycling buyers, the prospect of additional candidates remains encouraging, but there is still little evidence of a sustained increase in supply. Steel markets provided no common direction. Indian plate recovered from an early-week decline to finish at INR 43,300 per ton, while Bangladesh remained steady at BDT 66,000. Pakistan moved in the opposite direction, falling from PKR 195,000 to PKR 188,000 per ton. Chinese steel also softened marginally to USD 307.47 per ton. Despite these uneven fundamentals, improving sentiment and persistent candidate scarcity continue to support buying interest. Physical waterfront activity continued at Alang and Chattogram, with several previously secured vessels completing delivery, while Gadani reported no new movements. Bangladesh also received potentially important regulatory news, with the reported reclassification of ship recycling from the red to orange environmental category expected to simplify future yard approvals. The development has encouraged local sentiment, although implementation and environmental compliance considerations remain important. Bangladesh retains the strongest conventional buying appetite, Pakistan is becoming increasingly constructive despite weaker steel, and India continues to benefit from specialist opportunities. Turkey remains selective within its established regional market. Across the sub-continent, buyers are showing greater confidence, but freight earnings and second-hand alternatives continue to favour owners. The willingness to buy is growing. The willingness to sell remains the missing ingredient. For Week 44 of 2026, GMS Market Rankings / Vessel indications are as below. articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: The grid is the limit in International Shipping News 31/10/2026 A 41 MWh battery ferry entered service and a 151 MWh container ship design won approval this week, but the harder part is getting enough power to the quay. Battery-electric ships are moving beyond short-hop ferries. This week a 41 MWh ferry began crossing the River Plate, a fast ferry for the Strait of Gibraltar was launched, an electric barge was ordered for Vietnam and a 1,700 TEU battery container ship design was approved. Each depends on power ashore. Ferries first Ferry operator Buquebus’s China Zorrilla has begun sailing between Argentina and Uruguay with a 41 megawatt-hour (MWh) battery system. It can sail for up to 1.5 hours on battery power. Norwegian battery maker Corvus Energy, which supplied the system, said it is the largest marine battery installation currently in operation on a ship. Corvus said the installation has around four times the capacity of any battery previously fitted to a commercial vessel, and that the ferry is South America’s first fully electric ship of its kind. Australian shipbuilder Incat Tasmania built the vessel. Finnish technology company Wärtsilä picked Corvus in 2023 to supply the ferry’s battery system. “This project proves that battery-electric propulsion is no longer limited to smaller ferries or short routes,” said Ole Jacob Irgens, executive vice president and head of sales at Corvus. Spanish ferry operator Baleària has launched its first fully electric fast ferry at Armon Shipyards in Gijón, Spain. The 87-metre vessel has a 14 MWh battery system and is scheduled to start sailing between Tarifa in Spain and Tangier in Morocco in summer 2027. A second ferry, now under construction, is expected to join it later that year. The two will operate along the first green corridor between Spain and Morocco. Baleària has not disclosed the launched vessel’s name. From ferries to boxes The largest battery in the week’s news is still on paper. The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) has approved the concept design of a 1,700 TEU fully electric container ship developed by Hanwha Power, part of South Korean conglomerate Hanwha Group. The design runs entirely on a 151 MWh battery energy storage system, more than three times the capacity of China Zorrilla’s. The batteries sit in containerised units that can be handled and stowed like cargo containers, so they can be replaced, Hanwha Power said. The company sees the design as a potential pathway to decarbonising short-sea and regional container shipping. Even with batteries that can be lifted off like containers, the design relies on port charging to run without direct carbon emissions, Hanwha Power said. Hanwha Power has also completed the basic design of a 1,000 TEU battery-powered container ship. Batteries are heading for inland waterways too. Global sportswear company Nike has contracted French container shipping firm CMA CGM for a fully electric barge in Vietnam, which CMA CGM will operate with logistics and port operator Gemadept. The barge will link Nike’s inland drop-off location in Ho Chi Minh City with the Gemalink deep-sea terminal at Cai Mep. A potential strike threatening operations at some of the busiest container terminals in the United States has been pushed back after the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) and the International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 agreed to extend negotiations through November 4. PMA announced Friday that the two sides had signed an extension through 5 p.m. Pacific Time on Wednesday, November 4, avoiding a potential walkout that had been threatened for November 1. Negotiations will continue with assistance from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service. The dispute involves approximately 250 maritime watchmen represented by ILWU Local 26 who perform security-related duties at terminals throughout the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. Despite the relatively small number of workers involved, the potential disruption is significant. According to PMA, Local 26 members work at terminals handling roughly 85% of cargo moving through the Port of Long Beach and 33% at the Port of Los Angeles. As gCaptain previously reported , a strike could have consequences well beyond the watchmen themselves. PMA has warned that other ILWU workers are unlikely to cross Local 26 picket lines, potentially halting vessel, yard and gate operations at affected terminals. The union had identified eight terminal locations that could be affected by a walkout. The two sides have been negotiating a new agreement since the previous contract expired in July 2025. Local 26 has accused employers of failing to make meaningful progress, while PMA has maintained that significant differences remain despite more than a year of bargaining. “PMA remains committed to reaching a fair agreement at the bargaining table that avoids disruption at the nation’s two busiest ports,” the employer association said Friday. The extension provides several additional days for negotiators to reach an agreement, but the underlying labor dispute remains unresolved. The stakes are particularly high for the Southern California port complex, which handled a combined record 2.04 million twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in September. For now, the immediate strike threat has been postponed, with the next deadline set for Wednesday afternoon. articles.body: Chinese Stealth Drone Successfully Takes Off, Lands on Amphibious Assault Ship Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Frank Jr China's first carrier-based stealth reconnaissance and strike drone, the GJ-21, recently completed its first takeoff and landing on the Sichuan, the country's first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, state news agency Xinhua reported on Friday. The trial underscores Beijing's push to integrate drone technology into its military modernisation drive, a decades-long effort in which China has developed advanced warships, fighter jets, missiles and increasingly capable unmanned systems. Xinhua hailed the test as "a breakthrough in China's amphibious assault ship programme" and said it signifies the navy's ability to operate fixed-wing stealth drones from large naval platforms. GJ-21 first appeared at a military parade Beijing held last year to mark the 80th anniversary of the end of World War Two, where it displayed different types of weapons. State tabloid the Global Times reported on Friday that GJ-21 has a substantial combat radius despite having a smaller airframe than the stealthy J-35 and J-20 fighters, citing military expert Zhang Xuefeng. "GJ-21 is also low cost and reusable. Unlike hypersonic missiles, it can be recovered and redeployed multiple times. It can also deploy small, low-cost glide-guided bombs. Under high-tempo operations, it offers greater fire delivery efficiency with better cost control," Zhang was quoted as saying. The Sichuan, the lead vessel of China's Type 076 amphibious assault ship class, was launched in December 2024 and features electromagnetic catapult and arresting technology. It can carry fixed-wing drones, helicopters and amphibious equipment. The vessel has a full-load displacement of more than 40,000 metric tons and features a full-length flight deck and twin-island superstructure. China's state television CCTV said on Friday that the indigenously developed vessel conducted consecutive sea trials in late October. It did not disclose locations of the trials. China's navy said in April that the Sichuan sailed to waters in the South China Sea for scientific testing and training missions. It said at the time the deployment was a routine test and did not aim at any specific target. (Reuters)

articles.body: Dockworkers Strike Continues Friday Against Arms Shipments Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 © Adobe Stock/mangpink_s Dockworkers went on strike across Europe and beyond on Friday, disrupting shipping and ferries as they protested against the use of their ports for arms shipments and the number of seafarers killed in wars from the Gulf to the Black Sea. Strikers across 113 ports in 22 countries also called for pay rises, better working conditions and the right to have doctors on board vessels crossing war zones. "We will not work for their wars, and we will not become food for their cannons," Apostolos Kypraios, head of the Greek union of merchant marine engineers, told Reuters during a rally at the Greek port of Piraeus. 'SEAFARERS HAVE SUFFERED MANY CASUALTIES' "We have felt it first hand, and our families have felt it too, living with the anxiety of whether a colleague will get back home," he added. More than 25 unions have now backed the strike originally called in Italy, France, Greece, Spain's Basque Country, Turkey and Morocco. On Friday, it covered major shipping hubs in Piraeus, Valencia, Le Havre, Algeciras and Genoa, as well as Morocco's Tangier Med and India's Nhava Sheva. "Seafarers have suffered many casualties — numbering in the hundreds — including both the dead and the severely injured," the Greek seafarers' union PENEN said in a statement. It said there had been 28 attacks on vessels in the Gulf in the first 21 days of October, a record since the start of the Iran war. It said there had been 570 attacks confirmed in the Black Sea so far this year, leaving 40 seafarers dead and hundreds wounded. A series of strikes in the western Black Sea has raised concerns about the widening scope of Russia's war in Ukraine. Cargo operations were disrupted in Piraeus and ferry services to Greek islands were suspended, as about 3,000 dockworkers and seafarers joined the walkout. Representatives of India's WTWFI union said about 15 Indian seafarers had died as a result of the Iran war, with many more stranded at sea as waterways were blocked. A group of dockworkers and other activists, called 'No Harbour for Genocide' and campaigning to stop military cargo from reaching Israeli ports, said on Friday the protest would halt some 52,000 containers and snarl cargo worth $2.8 billion. Reuters was not able to independently verify the impact. In May 2026, dockworkers' unions from over 35 European countries published the so-called Istanbul Declaration demanding that port facilities not be used to transport weapons destined for war zones. Dockworkers said they were also worried about the rising cost of essential goods and energy, stemming from the ongoing conflicts. "We can't even afford to fill the car with fuel to get to the supermarket," George Gogos, head of the Piraeus port dockworkers' union, said. articles.body: Oil Leak Stopped From Tanker Offshore UAE, Clean Up Efforts Continue Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 Illustration © Yellow Boat / Adobe Stock The United Arab Emirates said on Friday that an oil leak from the Gem No. 2 tanker had been stopped, with no new leakage detected, as cleanup operations continued along coastlines affected by the spill. The oil slick is concentrated off the northern emirate of Umm Al Quwain and extends partly towards coastal areas in the neighbouring northern emirates of Ras Al Khaimah, Ajman and Sharjah, state news agency WAM reported, citing the environment ministry. The density of marine pollution has declined markedly, it added. Authorities have temporarily closed some beaches and coastal areas as a precaution, though the ministry said this did not necessarily mean pollution had been detected at every site affected by the closures. Environment ministry teams are carrying out field surveys, monitoring and cleanup operations in coastal areas reached by the pollution, in coordination with federal and local authorities, WAM said. Authorities have not said what caused the spill, but shipping sources have told Reuters the vessel was struck by a projectile on October 9, causing a fire that was later extinguished. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have driven up security risks for maritime traffic and heightened fears over the conflict's environmental fallout. Technical teams have repaired damaged parts of the tanker, restored some operating systems and are assessing the integrity of its structure to determine the safest way to handle it, WAM added, citing the energy ministry. The UAE also said fish and food products available in markets were safe for human consumption and that precautionary measures to protect drinking water supplies would not affect distribution. The country relies heavily on desalination plants for drinking water, while much of its economy, including ports and industrial facilities, is concentrated along its coastline, making marine contamination particularly sensitive. articles.summary: As gCaptain reported earlier this week, the Maritime Administration (MARAD) announced its approval of the $8.2 billion Texas ST LNG export port application, a major development for U.S. energy production. But the announcement also highlighted another significant milestone: the fastest deepwater port license review in...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Wojciech Wrzesien / Shutterstock By Tom Ewing (gCaptain) – As gCaptain reported earlier this week , the Maritime Administration (MARAD) announced its approval of the $8.2 billion Texas ST LNG export port application, a major development for U.S. energy production. But the announcement also highlighted another significant milestone: the fastest deepwater port license review in more than 20 years. According to the Department of Transportation (DOT) , the review was completed nearly 3.7 years faster than the historical average, representing a 70% reduction in review time. The acceleration follows changes implemented in January, when MARAD assumed the lead role in deepwater port reviews and the U.S. Coast Guard shifted to a supporting role focused on vessel operations, maritime safety and security. ST LNG filed its application with MARAD and the Coast Guard on June 9, 2025. Under the streamlined approach, MARAD completed the Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS) in just 410 days. DOT credited the changes with eliminating unnecessary administrative procedures and accelerating the review process. In response to DOT’s announcement, gCaptain followed up with questions seeking additional insight into which specific changes had the greatest impact on reducing red tape. A DOT spokesperson, speaking on background, said “the primary efficiency gained was fixing a structural inefficiency, rather than addressing challenges within any specific partner agency.” Previously, MARAD and the U.S. Coast Guard operated under a co-lead structure for reviews required by the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). DOT’s spokesperson said this shared responsibility for environmental reviews “inadvertently created duplicative administrative steps, parallel document routing, and sequential reviews.” Now, with MARAD serving as the sole lead agency, project schedules have been consolidated and the review team has established a unified approach to interagency communication. “The U.S. Coast Guard remains an important partner in this process,” DOT explained, adding that “this shift simply allows them to focus purely on their core statutory missions of maritime safety, security, and operational risk assessment, while MARAD drives the environmental timeline.” The Coast Guard is listed in the project’s Record of Decision (ROD) as one of six federal cooperating agencies, but the document does not otherwise include or reference specific Coast Guard statements. Neither U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Region 6 nor the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, two other federal partners, filed objections or concerns regarding application approval. The deepwater port development will consist of four phases. Each phase includes five fixed offshore platforms (Gas Treatment, Liquefaction, Bridge Support Trestle, LNG Transfer, and Accommodation and Utilities), bridges linking the platforms, a dolphin mooring system composed of three berthing dolphins and six mooring dolphins, and a moored LNG Floating Storage Unit (FSU). At full build-out, the deepwater port will include 20 platforms, four FSUs, four mooring systems, and 7.7 miles of pipeline, consisting of a 5.6-mile lateral pipeline and 2.1 miles of interconnecting pipelines between the phases. DOT was asked whether the ST LNG project benefited from any one-time procedural exemptions that might not apply to future projects. DOT’s answer: No. Going forward, MARAD’s leadership role and the related procedural steps will follow the changes formally established in January. DOT was also asked to identify the types of red tape that have historically impeded timely reviews, such as repetitive filings or demands for unnecessary information. The spokesperson said the primary efficiency came from eliminating duplicative administrative procedures. Under the previous co-lead model, draft environmental documents, requests for information and legal reviews often had to move sequentially between multiple agencies before they could advance or be published. “By consolidating the NEPA (National Environmental Policy Act) process under MARAD,” DOT said, “we established a single Federal docket and a unified project management team. We eliminated redundant legal and administrative processing, aligned our public comment periods, and streamlined how cooperating agencies provide input.” Finally, DOT was asked about environmental reviews that must proceed according to nature’s timetable, such as studies involving temperature cycles, migration patterns or other seasonal factors. Were there opportunities to streamline reviews of environmental processes that inherently take weeks or months to evaluate? DOT replied: “Streamlining our administrative process does not mean cutting corners on rigorous environmental science or biological mandates.” To manage extended seasonal or biological studies efficiently, the spokesperson said MARAD is “front-loading” interagency coordination. MARAD’s team is engaging cooperating agencies, such as NOAA Fisheries, earlier in the scoping and pre-application phases to identify required biological studies as soon as possible. MARAD is also seeking to maximize the use of existing regional data from prior offshore projects to satisfy baseline requirements where appropriate, reducing the need for duplicative studies conducted from scratch. DOT noted that “when project-specific seasonal data collection is legally required, we integrate those study schedules into a predictable, concurrent review timeline rather than letting them cause cascading, sequential delays. This approach ensures we maintain the exact same statutory level of environmental assurance while drastically reducing idle administrative time in the schedule.” To be clear, MARAD’s application approval is not the same as the issuance of a license to operate. In fact, MARAD’s approval is conditional. ST LNG must agree in writing not to make changes to its deepwater port application and must demonstrate compliance with nine conditions before a license can be issued. Those conditions cover matters ranging from financial responsibility and oil spill liability to eventual decommissioning. The required compliance documentation must be submitted at least 90 days before a license can be issued. articles.summary: Hanwha Philly Shipyard has secured a $269 million contract to build a Medium Landing Ship (LSM) for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, marking a major milestone in the South...
