(Image: U.S. Navy) Hanwha Philly Shipyard has secured a $269 million contract to build a Medium Landing Ship (LSM) for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps, marking a major milestone in the South Korean company’s push into U.S. naval shipbuilding. TOTE Services announced Friday that it selected Hanwha Defense USA (HDUSA) as the first shipbuilder under its $2.2 billion Vessel Construction Manager (VCM) contract for the LSM program. The award covers construction of one vessel at the Philadelphia shipyard, with options for three additional ships. Construction is expected to begin in the fourth quarter of 2027, with the program’s first vessel scheduled for delivery in 2030. The selection follows a competitive bidding process launched in July and comes just days after Hanwha announced plans to place its Philadelphia shipyard under the control of its U.S. defense subsidiary. “Since acquiring Philly Shipyard in 2024, Hanwha has made significant investments in its workforce and technology to pave the way to build ships for the U.S. Navy and other federal customers,” said HDUSA President and CEO Michael Coulter. The contract represents Hanwha Defense USA’s first U.S. Navy shipbuilding award and a significant step in the company’s effort to transform the former commercial shipyard into a dual-use facility serving both military and commercial customers. TOTE Services said Hanwha was selected based on its competitive pricing and acceptance of subcontract terms and conditions. The company is also continuing contract discussions with Bollinger Shipyards and Fincantieri Marinette Marine, which are expected to participate in construction of the LSM fleet. “This award shows the speed at which the VCM model can move from RFP to contract,” said TOTE Services President Jeff Dixon. “Through a competitive process, we secured strong terms that benefit the government, along with build positions that allow construction to start in the fourth quarter of 2027.” The LSM program is intended to provide the Marine Corps with smaller amphibious vessels capable of transporting personnel, equipment and supplies between islands and coastal locations, particularly in the Indo-Pacific. The Navy and Marine Corps are planning a fleet of 35 vessels, with TOTE’s initial contract covering up to eight ships. The award also builds on an existing relationship between TOTE Services and the Philadelphia yard. Under a separate VCM arrangement with the U.S. Maritime Administration, TOTE has overseen construction of the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel (NSMV) program at Philly Shipyard. Four of the five training ships have already been delivered. “Hanwha Philly Shipyard has already built and delivered four National Security Multi-Mission Vessels under the VCM model with TOTE Services, and we will leverage that experience to deliver the LSM to the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps,” said Tim Glinatsis, senior vice president of program management at HDUSA. The announcement comes amid a broader restructuring of Hanwha’s U.S. shipbuilding operations. As gCaptain recently reported , Hanwha Defense USA announced this week that it is acquiring a controlling stake in Hanwha Philly Shipyard, shifting the facility toward defense-led ownership as the company expands its U.S. naval shipbuilding business. Hanwha acquired the shipyard in December 2024 and has since been investing in workforce development, infrastructure and technology to support an expansion into naval construction. The shift has also raised questions about the future balance between military and commercial shipbuilding at one of the country’s major Jones Act shipyards. Asked by gCaptain whether Hanwha would maintain and expand commercial Jones Act shipbuilding capacity as the yard transitions toward defense-led ownership, a company spokesperson said it was “in a good position to compete and build for commercial and naval demand as a dual-use yard.” Friday’s contract announcement provides the clearest indication yet of how Hanwha intends to put that strategy into practice, establishing a foothold in Navy ship construction while positioning the Philadelphia facility to compete for additional government and commercial work. articles.title: Grimaldi Warns U.S. Port Fees Could Force Ships Out of American Trades
articles.summary: Italian shipping giant Grimaldi Group is warning that reinstating U.S. port fees on foreign-built vehicle carriers could force it to redeploy vessels away from American trades, potentially disrupting shipping services...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Grimaldi Group Italian shipping giant Grimaldi Group is warning that reinstating U.S. port fees on foreign-built vehicle carriers could force it to redeploy vessels away from American trades, potentially disrupting shipping services for U.S. exporters and automakers. In an October 30 filing with the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) , Grimaldi strongly backed the Trump administration’s proposal to extend the suspension of Section 301 port fees through January 9, 2027. The company went a step further, calling for a permanent suspension of the fees targeting foreign-built vehicle carriers. “Many of our American customers have expressed concern at the thought of Grimaldi redeploying its ships out of US trades if the proposed further suspension of this Section 301 action is not implemented,” the company said. The warning comes as USTR considers a two-month extension of the existing suspension , which is scheduled to expire November 9. The proposed extension would keep the measures on hold through January 9, 2027, while Washington and Beijing continue negotiations over China’s dominance of global shipbuilding. Grimaldi, one of the world’s largest operators of roll-on/roll-off, container and pure car and truck carriers, argued that the fees could have unintended consequences for American businesses that depend on its services. The company pointed to its cargo volumes over the past three years, reporting nearly 985,000 tons of U.S. exports and 1.31 million tons of imports. According to Grimaldi, 74.7% of its U.S. import volume consisted of cargo belonging to American automakers. In total, the company said 86% of the cargo it carries in U.S. trades consists of American exports or imports associated with U.S. automakers. “Few shipping lines have such a high percentage of American cargo,” Grimaldi said. The company also highlighted its longstanding relationship with the United States, noting that it has called at American ports since 2001 and supplied cargo ships to the U.S. Navy during the Second Gulf War. The filing adds to growing concerns among international shipping companies over the potential return of Section 301 fees, which were introduced last year as part of Washington’s effort to counter China’s dominance of the global maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors. The measures initially took effect on October 14, 2025, before being suspended on November 10 as part of a broader trade agreement between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The fees target Chinese-owned and Chinese-operated vessels, Chinese-built ships and certain foreign-built vehicle carriers. Although intended to strengthen American shipbuilding, the measures have faced criticism from carriers that argue they could increase transportation costs and disrupt established shipping networks. Grimaldi’s warning follows similar concerns raised by Atlantic Container Line (ACL), whose CEO Andy Abbott told gCaptain last week that customers feared the carrier would redeploy ships away from U.S. trades if the fees returned. “ACL’s unique ships were mistakenly classified by USTR as vehicle carriers even though only 1% of its cargo is automobiles,” Abbott said. “Our largest US container and heavy machinery customers were panicking that we would redeploy our ships out of the US trade to the booming China trade.” The concerns from Grimaldi and ACL highlight a potential conflict between Washington’s efforts to rebuild domestic shipbuilding and the interests of American exporters that rely on foreign-built ships to move their cargo. The administration’s proposed extension has also faced opposition from lawmakers and maritime labor groups that want the fees reinstated. In June, Senators Mark Kelly and Elizabeth Warren urged USTR to restore the charges, arguing that their suspension undermined efforts to rebuild U.S. commercial shipbuilding and deprived the government of potential revenue for maritime investments. For Grimaldi, however, the issue goes beyond a temporary extension. The company is calling for permanent relief from the fees imposed under Annex III of the Section 301 action, which specifically addresses foreign-built vehicle carriers. “Grimaldi understands the intentions of USTR to advance policies that strengthen US national security and manufacturing/agricultural/maritime competitiveness,” the company said. But it added that it hopes “no insurmountable roadblocks will be put in our way.” The USTR public comment period closes October 30 at 5 p.m. Eastern Time. The proposed two-month extension has not yet been finalized. articles.title: TOTE Services Selects Hanwha Defense USA for Medium Landing Ship Program
articles.summary: TOTE Services, LLC, a U.S. maritime services company specializing in vessel construction management and ship management, announced its first shipyard selection, Hanwha Defense USA (HDUS), for the Medium Landing Ship (LSM) program under TOTE…
articles.body: TOTE Services Selects Hanwha Defense USA for Medium Landing Ship Program Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 © TOTE Services TOTE Services, LLC, a U.S. maritime services company specializing in vessel construction management and ship management, announced its first shipyard selection, Hanwha Defense USA (HDUS), for the Medium Landing Ship (LSM) program under TOTE Services’ Vessel Construction Manager (VCM) contract for the U.S. Navy and Marine Corps. As VCM for the LSM program, TOTE Services issued a request for proposals (RFP) to qualified U.S. shipyards in July 2026. The award covers construction of one LSM, valued at $269 million, at Hanwha Philly Shipyard (HPSI), with options for three additional vessels. The program will include up to eight new vessels under the base contract. TOTE Services continues productive contract discussions with Bollinger Shipyards and Fincantieri Marinette Marine, both directed shipyards under the VCM contract, which are expected to play a meaningful role in building the LSM fleet. TOTE Services’ $2.2 billion VCM contract supports the Navy and Marine Corps’ planned 35-ship LSM fleet. The first vessel is expected to deliver in 2030. TOTE Services will provide one accountable management structure connecting government requirements to shipyard execution across three domestic shipbuilders, helping to accelerate delivery, strengthen cost and schedule discipline, and expand the U.S. shipbuilding industrial base. That work includes standardizing configuration across the fleet, using block buys to secure favorable pricing, and delivering vessels in a timely manner. TOTE Services pioneered the VCM model in U.S. government shipbuilding through its work on the National Security Multi-Mission Vessel program for the U.S. Maritime Administration. As VCM for the five-vessel program, TOTE Services has overseen shipyard selection, design, construction, testing, delivery, and lifecycle logistics. Four vessels have been delivered, with the fifth, Golden State, expected in 2027. The LSM award builds on that work at Hanwha Philly Shipyard, where an experienced workforce and established supply chain position the yard to begin construction quickly. Beyond the ships themselves, the LSM program can provide a more reliable demand signal for American shipyards, suppliers, manufacturers and skilled trades, helping the industrial base plan, invest and build with greater consistency.

articles.title: Portchain Acquired by StormGeo, Advancing Just-in-Time Voyage Optimization
articles.summary: StormGeo, part of Alfa Laval, has acquired Portchain, a provider of berth alignment software connecting terminals and carriers through shared, real-time port call data. The acquisition adds port call coordination to StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence…
articles.body: Portchain Acquired by StormGeo, Advancing Just-in-Time Voyage Optimization Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 Just-In Time port call coordination with Portchain. © Portchain/StormGeo StormGeo, part of Alfa Laval, has acquired Portchain, a provider of berth alignment software connecting terminals and carriers through shared, real-time port call data. The acquisition adds port call coordination to StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence, creating the foundation for a new approach to Just-in-Time voyage optimization at scale. The goal is to connect decisions about route and speed with the latest information on berth availability and terminal plans, helping operators respond to changes while a vessel is still at sea. Portchain connects container carriers and terminals through shared operational data. Portchain Connect supports digital alignment of vessel schedules and cargo volumes, while Portchain Quay supports berth, crane and workforce planning in a shared, real-time environment. Today, the Portchain Network connects shipping lines with more than 200 terminals, representing over 40% of global container terminal capacity. StormGeo’s Voyage Intelligence combines voyage optimization, vessel-performance insight and expert route guidance to help operators optimize for arrival time, fuel consumption or the balance between the two. Portchain adds a shared, real-time view of berth plans aligned with terminal operators and their resources. As the companies develop this combined offering, a change in the expected berth time could inform speed decisions while the vessel is still at sea. Operators could reassess the voyage plan and better align the vessel’s estimated time of arrival (ETA) with its estimated time of berthing (ETB). Updated arrival information will also help terminals plan berths, cranes and teams. This is the foundation for Just-in-Time voyage optimization at scale: turning a change in the terminal plan into a timely voyage decision. The aim is to help vessels arrive closer to when the terminal is ready to receive them, reducing avoidable waiting, fuel use and emissions while making arrivals more predictable. The acquisition advances StormGeo’s ambition to connect weather, vessel and port insights in support of more efficient and predictable maritime operations. Together with Alfa Laval’s marine portfolio, it supports customers’ efforts to improve operational efficiency and progress towards decarbonization. The addition also strengthens Alfa Laval’s offering across the fuel transition and energy efficiency by adding StormGeo’s expertise in routing and port call coordination, with digitalization and AI helping to simplify maritime operations. Portchain will operate as an independent company under StormGeo for the next few years and will later be fully integrated into StormGeo’s portfolio. Existing Portchain customers will see no disruption to their service, and the combined offering will be available through StormGeo.

articles.title: ClassNK Releases Second Edition of Cyber Security Management Guidelines
articles.summary: ClassNK has released the second edition of its "Guidelines for Cyber Security Management System for Ships." Intended for shipowners and ship management companies, the guidelines set out the requirements for a Cyber Security Management System (CSMS)…
articles.body: ClassNK Releases Second Edition of Cyber Security Management Guidelines Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 © ClassNK ClassNK has released the second edition of its "Guidelines for Cyber Security Management System for Ships." Intended for shipowners and ship management companies, the guidelines set out the requirements for a Cyber Security Management System (CSMS), through which a Company addresses the cyber risks associated with ship operations as part of its day-to-day work, from governance and responsibilities ashore and onboard to the technical controls applied to shipboard systems. The Guidelines also make ClassNK’s certification audits transparent by showing the assessment criteria applied in them. In audits, ClassNK looks at the governance behind a company’s cyber security: policy and management commitment, defined roles and responsibilities, risk assessment, implementation and operation of controls, and preparedness for incidents. The second edition has been restructured with reference to ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27002, and the assessment criteria for each CSMS requirement have been clarified. The requirements have also been mapped to the cyber security requirements of major vetting schemes. Cyber security is increasingly covered in the external assessments conducted by maritime stakeholders, and many of those requirements focus on how cyber risk is managed. A CSMS certified against these guidelines gives companies an objective means of demonstrating that governance to external stakeholders, and a single foundation for responding to multiple vetting requirements. Background The IMO recommends that cyber risks be managed within the Safety Management Systems under the ISM Code. In response, ClassNK published the first edition of the Guidelines in 2019, setting out CSMS requirements built on the framework of the ISM Code, and has since been providing CSMS certification based on the guidelines. As a collective effort of the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS), the application of IACS UR E26 and E27 has defined the cyber resilience capabilities that ships and their onboard systems must have from the newbuild phase. At the same time, a vessel’s operating environment keeps changing throughout its service life, as the systems are updated and operations and organizations change. Addressing cyber risks is therefore not a matter of technical measures alone; continuous management is essential to select, implement, maintain and review those measures appropriately. In recent years, cyber risk management covering practices such as access control, software updates, education and training, and incident response have also become a part of the assessment criteria as part of the subject to the schemes established by DryBMS, OCIMF, RightShip and others, each with their own criteria. The first edition offered the elements for establishing a CSMS as a high-level objective, leaving each Company to interpret how to achieve them within its own organization. Putting those elements into practice requires wide efforts across the whole Company, from shore-based organizations to shipboard operations, and time to achieve. Through its audits since 2019, ClassNK has built up practical knowledge of what effective implementation looks like. Drawing on that experience, the second edition makes clear what is verified in audits and has been designed with other external assessments in mind, so that a CSMS built on the guidelines also prepares a company to meet them. Main revisions Clarification of audit criteria, structured with reference to international standards The guidelines now consist of two parts: Part 1 sets out the CSMS requirements, and Part 2 specifies the audit criteria and the objective evidence required for each requirement. This allows companies to understand in advance what will be verified in audits and prepare accordingly, and makes it easier to identify where there is room for improvement in their own practices. Mapping to external assessment criteria set by major industry bodies The assessment criteria in Part 2 have also been mapped against the cyber security requirements or benchmarks of major vetting bodies (covering RISQ, SIRE 2.0, DryBMS and TMSA*3). Rather than interpreting each scheme separately, Companies can use the CSMS as a common framework for meeting them and can expect the reduction of the time and burden needed for compliance. ClassNK will continue to support cyber security efforts in the maritime industry through the provision of guidelines as well as audits and certification. How to access guidelines The guidelines are available to download via "Guidelines" of My Page on ClassNK’s website after registration: ClassNK MyPage Login

articles.title: Corn Belt Ports See Notable Freight Tonnage Growth in 2026
articles.summary: In the most recent annual report released by the U.S. Waterborne Commerce Statistics Center, two Corn Belt Ports regions took top honors for showing some of the highest growth rates in the inland waterway port system. The Mid-America Port Commission (IL…
articles.body: Corn Belt Ports See Notable Freight Tonnage Growth in 2026 Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 © Corn Belt Ports In the most recent annual report released by the U.S. Waterborne Commerce Statistics Center, two Corn Belt Ports regions took top honors for showing some of the highest growth rates in the inland waterway port system. The Mid-America Port Commission (IL, MO, IA), established in 1999, was ranked as the 40th largest port in the U.S., and saw a 15.2% growth in freight tonnage during the 2024 reporting year (published 2026). This is the highest growth rate for any large (Top 50) U.S. Inland Port. The Illinois Waterway Ports Commission established in 2023, and now reported as a port statistical area in the report, saw a 5.9% increase in freight tonnage, the largest increase of any port statistical area in the U.S. In the report the Upper Mississippi River (Marine Highway 35) saw a 4.2% increase, and the Illinois River (Marine Highway 55 NORTH) saw a 1.2% increase in freight tonnage overall. The Corn Belt Ports are special districts of government or official government collaborations. They are the modern, sustainable, rural, regional, inland, partnership ports on the Upper Mississippi River (Marine Highway 35) and the Illinois River (Marine Highway 35 NORTH) inside of the lock and dam system recognized by the U.S. Congress as the Upper Mississippi River and Illinois Waterway System. The Corn Belt Ports consist of the Illinois Waterway Ports Commission, the Mid-America Port Commission, the Upper Mississippi River Ports of Eastern lowa and Western Illinois, and the Northern Grain Belt Ports. articles.body: Sanmar Hands Over New Harbour Tug for Bulgaria's Black Sea Port Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 KASTRITSI tug (Credit: Sanmar Shipyards) Turkish shipbuilder Sanmar Shipyards has delivered a new harbour tugboat to Bulgarian operator VTC S.A., marking the fifth vessel supplied to the company since their partnership began in 2003. The tug, renamed KASTRITSI by its new owner, will join VTC's fleet at the Black Sea port of Varna, supporting harbour towage and marine operations. Based on the RApport 2500 design by Robert Allan, KASTRITSI is a shallow-draft Azimuth Stern Drive (ASD) tug designed for operations in confined and shallow waterways. The vessel measures 25.2 meters in length and 12 meters in beam, with a maximum draught of 4.2 meters, ahead bollard pull exceeding 50 tonnes and a maximum speed of 12 knots. It is also equipped with FiFi-1 firefighting capability and accommodation for six crew members. Sanmar's engagement with VTC dates back to 2003, when the shipbuilder supplied three twin-screw tugs, SANMAR XII, SANMAR XIII and SANMAR XIV. A fourth tug, TICHA, based on Robert Allan's RApport 1600SX design, followed in 2018. "We have been working with VTC since the very beginning of its operations in 2003, and we are proud of the relationship we have built over more than two decades. The delivery of KASTRITSI marks another important step in our cooperation, and we are delighted to see her join the VTC fleet in Varna," said Cem Seven, Chairman of Sanmar Shipyards. VTC provides harbour towage and marine services in the Bulgarian ports of Varna and Balchik, including vessel assistance, berthing and unberthing, coastal and offshore towage, and emergency response.

articles.body: General Dynamics' Backlog Surges to $220B on Major Defense Orders Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. October 30, 2026 (Credit: General Dynamics) General Dynamics reported $98.8 billion in new orders in the third quarter of 2026, driven by major submarine contracts, while revenue rose 12.9% year-on-year to $14.6 billion, the company announced on October 30. The aerospace and defense company's total backlog reached $220.3 billion at the end of the quarter, with an additional $50.4 billion in estimated potential contract value, bringing its total estimated contract value to $270.7 billion. Orders across its defense segments totaled $93.8 billion, driven by large contracts for Virginia- and Columbia-class submarines in its Marine Systems business, while the Aerospace segment secured $5 billion in orders. The company's book-to-bill ratio, which measures orders received relative to revenue, reached 6.8 for the quarter, including 8.5 across its defense segments and 1.4 in Aerospace. General Dynamics reported operating earnings of $1.5 billion, up 14.7% from the same period last year, while diluted earnings per share increased 15.7% to $4.49. Operating margin improved by 20 basis points to 10.5%. “Our business had exceptional third quarter results, with revenue growth across all four segments, robust bookings and solid operational performance,” said Phebe Novakovic, chairman and chief executive officer of General Dynamics. “With the consistent growth in our backlog and our significant investment in our businesses over the last decade, we are poised to drive continued performance in the years to come.” Cash from operating activities totaled $1.7 billion, representing 139% of net earnings. During the quarter, General Dynamics invested $481 million in capital expenditures, paid $429 million in dividends and reduced its total debt by $500 million. The company ended the quarter with $7 billion in total debt and $4.4 billion in cash and equivalents.

MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Noble Intrepid jack-up rig Source: Noble Corporation U.S.-headquartered offshore drilling contractor Noble Corporation is fueling its fleet utilization uptick with multimillion-dollar drilling assignments off the coasts of Uruguay, Nigeria, Ghana, Peru, and Norway, enabling its total contract backlog to hit $6.7 billion in the third quarter of 2026. With new contract wins of approximately $560 million awarded since the July fleet status report, Noble’s backlog as of October 26, 2026, stands at $6.7 billion, excluding mobilization and demobilization revenue. The firm's fleet of 23 marketed floaters was 66% contracted during the third quarter compared with 64% in the prior quarter, while recent contract awards added around 44 months of new floater backlog, with leading edge day rates for Tier-1 drillships ranging between the mid-$400,000s and $500,000. The utilization of Noble's five marketed ultra-harsh jack-ups was 86% in the third quarter versus 80% during the prior quarter, while latest contract awards brought approximately 26 months of new jack-up backlog, with leading edge day rates ranging between $230,000 and $300,000. " The third quarter, which featured a 5% sequential decrease in adjusted EBITDA, marked the successful resumption of operations for both of our rigs in Brazil, but was also impacted by several other rigs across the fleet transitioning between contracts. On the commercial front, we have recently secured approximately $560 million in new contract awards, including a number of key programs that support a strengthening fleet utilization profile as we move through 2027. " — Robert Eifler Noble's Chief Executive Officer (CEO) The 2014-built Noble BlackHawk drillship has secured one-well contract with Apache Corporation in Uruguay , which is expected to begin in Q4 2027, with an estimated duration of 50 days. This contract award of approximately $25 million excludes additional fees for mobilization and demobilization. The 2014-built Noble BlackRhino drillship has landed a four-well deal with TotalEnergies in Nigeria , which is anticipated to start in Q4 2026, with an estimated duration of 150 days plus six priced option wells. The 2013-built Noble Faye Kozack drillship has won a five-well assignment with Tullow Oil in Ghana , which is slated to commence in mid-2027, with an estimated duration of 250 days. This contract also comes with five priced option wells. The 2011-built Noble Globetrotter I drillship has picked up a two-well contract with Oxy in Peru , which is scheduled to kick off in Q2 2027. Terms of the contract, which includes additional fees for mobilization and demobilization, are not disclosed. Afterward, this rig is expected to embark on its contract with TotalEnergies in West Africa under a three-year capacity reservation agreement (CRA) for light well intervention services, providing a minimum commitment of 150 days per year, with first call-off service order set to start in Angola in Q3/Q4 2027. The 2014-built Noble Interceptor jack-up rig has obtained a one-well contract with DNO in Norway , which is anticipated to begin in Q3 2027, with an estimated duration of 50-90 days. As a result, the rig is expected to kick off, in direct continuation, a long-term plug and abandonment (P&A) scope for ConocoPhillips in Norway on the Ekofisk field , with an estimated duration of 670 days. The 2014-built Noble Intrepid jack-up rig has been hired on a one-well assignment with Orlen in Norway, which is due to commence in Q3 2027, with an estimated duration of 40-60 days. articles.body: Interconnectors October 30, 2026 · 1 day ago €3.1 billion Spain-France interconnector is 70% complete NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Red Eléctrica The multibillion-euro Biscay Gulf interconnector, set to increase electricity exchange capacity between Spain and France from 2.8 GW to 5 GW, is 70% complete, with onshore cable laying currently underway. Spanish transmission system operator (TSO) Red Eléctrica has begun underground cable laying for the electrical interconnection project that will, across the Bay of Biscay, connect Gatika in Spain and France's Cubnezais. The underground HVDC cables will run for 13 kilometers, from the Gatika converter station to the coast at Lemoiz, where they will connect to the submarine cables. Furthermore, Red Eléctrica recently completed the second phase of subsea cable laying, a 50-kilometer stretch, using Prysmian's cable-laying vessel (CLV) Monna Lisa. On the Biscayan coast, the first phase was completed in August with NKT's CLV Victoria, which was responsible for installing the first 65 kilometers of the route. With this, all the submarine cables have been installed in the Biscay section of the submarine interconnection. Work will continue on the sections off the coast of Gipuzkoa between November and February, with all sections expected to be laid in French waters until the summer. The Spanish TSO also reported that the construction of the future Gatika converter station is progressing well, with civil engineering work completed and the electromechanical assembly currently underway. The Biscay Gulf interconnector is now 70% complete. Developed by Red Eléctrica and its French counterpart RTE, through the joint venture Inelfe, the project is considered a Project of Common Interest by the European Union and is co-financed through CINEA - the European Union's Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency, in addition to support from the European Investment Bank (EIB). articles.summary: One of the largest coordinated port labour mobilisations in history is underway today, with more than 25 unions staging strikes and demonstrations at 113 ports across 22 countries and territories. articles.body: Ports and Logistics Dockworkers unite across 113 ports in global anti-war protest Sam Chambers October 30, 2026 0 2,184 1 minute read CGT CGT One of the largest coordinated port labour mobilisations in history is underway today, with more than 25 unions staging strikes and demonstrations at 113 ports across 22 countries and territories. The worldwide action, organised under the banner “Dockworkers do not work for war”, has expanded dramatically from a smaller mobilisation involving 20 ports across seven countries in February. Major gateways involved include Hamburg, Le Havre, Marseille, Genoa, Gioia Tauro, Piraeus, Tangier Med, Mersin and India’s Nhava Sheva. France’s CGT has called a 24-hour walkout across approximately 24 ports, predicting that as much as 95% of national port activity could be halted. Italy has registered a nationwide 24-hour ports strike, coinciding with a general strike affecting other transport sectors. In Greece, seafarers’ unions have called 24-hour stoppages expected to disrupt ferry services at Piraeus, Rafina, Lavrio, Patras and Igoumenitsa. Organisers estimate that participating unions represent workers handling around 40% of Mediterranean container traffic, with up to 40,000 containers potentially delayed.< However, the actual disruption remains uncertain. Some ports are holding demonstrations rather than stopping cargo operations, while Genoa’s port authority anticipates relatively limited disruption. The campaign primarily opposes military cargo shipments through civilian ports, alongside demands for improved wages, working conditions and protections against automation. Although unprecedented in scale for this particular campaign, claims that it is the world’s largest port strike remain unverified. An international solidarity campaign for Liverpool dockworkers in January 1997 involved 105 ports and cities across 27 countries. No further worldwide coordinated strike date has been announced. Separately, a potential November 1 strike involving 250 port watchmen threatens operations at Los Angeles and Long Beach, although negotiations to avert the stoppage are continuing. Italy also faces another national general strike on November 20.
